architectural_implications.after: Harness/config becomes a versioned artifact pinned alongside the model, and eval runs execute inside the exact production scaffold rather than a generic runner.
architectural_implications.before: Harness treated as a disposable test scaffold; model chosen from public leaderboards and then dropped into a custom production runtime.
architectural_implications.consequence: Configurations are versioned and regression-tested as units; upgrading either the model or the harness requires re-running the paired eval matrix because the ranking may invert.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluation harness determines model rankings, so the harness is effectively part of the system under test.

architectural_implications.after: Tool layer emits stage-tagged spans (requested, executed, returned payload, agent's stated interpretation) with separate injection points for search-limit and known-evidence tests.
architectural_implications.before: Trace review is post-hoc log reading; failures are diagnosed from the final answer and a flat log of tool calls.
architectural_implications.consequence: Per-stage fault attribution becomes automatable; instrumentation cost moves into the tool abstraction boundary, and 'agent failed' gets replaced by a specific stage and remediation.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent failures decompose into availability, invocation, return, and interpretation stages.

architectural_implications.after: Instrumentation asserts required-tool invocation and non-empty evidence independently of cost/score, making mechanism conformance a separate pass/fail dimension.
architectural_implications.before: Optimization targets observed cost and primary eval score; tool usage assumed to follow from task success.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cheap-but-broken configurations get rejected before deployment; cost becomes a valid target only within the set of configurations that satisfy mechanism invariants.
architectural_implications.observation: Cost and quality metrics can move in opposite directions from actual correctness.

architectural_implications.after: Approval becomes a blocking dependency that the tool-call path cannot bypass; audit queue holds executing work in suspension.
architectural_implications.before: Gate implemented as warning emission into a log or audit queue reviewed later.
architectural_implications.consequence: Latency and throughput now include human review time by construction, which must be modeled in the capacity plan rather than discovered in production incidents.
architectural_implications.observation: Approval gates must block execution rather than record it.

connections.relationship: A score is a property of the (model, harness) pair, so leaderboard validity is bounded by how closely the leaderboard harness matches the target deployment harness.
Stage decomposition (unavailable / uncalled / unreturned / misinterpreted) defines the span granularity required in the tool-call trace.
Whether the agent can distinguish 'no matches' from 'search failed' is a property of the tool's return schema, not only of the model.
Human review only changes system behavior when approval is a blocking dependency of tool invocation rather than an emitted log event.
Aggregate eval scores are only interpretable when task families (bug fixing vs. feature building) are scored and weighted explicitly rather than pooled.

evidence_quotes.text: Model rankings change dramatically when you switch the evaluation harness.
Astra outperforming Opus 5 when using the PI harness versus OpenHands
You must evaluate the specific configuration you will actually run in production.

core_insights.generalization: Any non-deterministic system whose performance is mediated by an external controller (orchestrator, runtime, tool layer) has capability that is only defined jointly with that controller; benchmark scores are properties of configurations, not of components.
core_insights.insight: Evaluation results are dominated by the harness-model pairing, not the model alone: the same benchmark produces different winners depending on the scaffold wrapping the model.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It invalidates using third-party leaderboards to select a model for a custom runtime. The scaffold (tool loop, prompting, context handling, retry logic) is a first-class variable that interacts with model weights, so a model's measured capability is only meaningful conditional on a specific harness. Engineers must evaluate the exact production configuration rather than a nominally identical model.

evidence_quotes.text: A 28% drop in observed cost does not mean the agent successfully used the intended tool.
Agents often trust empty tool results rather than realizing evidence is missing.
A 28% reduction in observed cost on code search tasks while the agent missed relevant evidence and trusted empty results.

core_insights.generalization: Any efficiency metric becomes gameable by removing work; pair every cost/latency objective with a mechanism-verification assertion (was the tool called, was evidence returned, was it cited) that the optimizer cannot satisfy by abstaining.
core_insights.insight: Cost reduction is a proxy metric that can be inversely correlated with correctness: a prompt change cut observed cost 28% while the agent silently stopped invoking the search tool and accepted empty results as ground truth.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Optimizing on cost/latency without a tool-utilization invariant lets agents 'succeed' cheaply by skipping the expensive evidence-gathering step. The failure is silent because the metric improves and no error is raised, so it will not surface in dashboards. Production systems need an assertion that required tools were actually called, independent of the cost/score metrics.

evidence_quotes.text: You need to test search limits and known-relevant evidence separately to see if evidence is actually used.
Better evidence can still go unused if the agent or harness fails to leverage it.
Enables engineers to debug where in the pipeline an agent fails—whether information was unavailable, uncalled, unreturned, or misinterpreted.

core_insights.generalization: Treat every retrieval-augmented or tool-using system as a staged data pipeline with per-stage instrumentation and per-stage injections, rather than scoring only the terminal output.
core_insights.insight: Agent failure requires positional diagnosis along an evidence pipeline — evidence was unavailable, uncalled, unreturned, or misinterpreted — and each stage must be tested with a separate ablation (search-limits test vs. known-relevant-evidence test).
core_insights.why_it_matters: It converts a monolithic 'agent failed' signal into four distinct, separately testable fault classes with different fixes: expand retrieval limits, fix tool selection, fix the tool's return contract, or fix the agent's interpretation of results. Without the split test you cannot tell whether better evidence would even help, since better evidence can be ignored.

evidence_quotes.text: Pulling in too many files (low precision) can result in high recall while failing business needs.
Grepping 295 files when only 6 were needed.

core_insights.generalization: Evaluation metrics are alignment artifacts: the scoring rule selects the agent's behavior, so the rule must be derived from the business cost of each error type, not inherited from a generic benchmark.
core_insights.insight: Scoring function choice determines whether an eval measures business success: high recall achieved by over-fetching (grepping 295 files to find 6) can pass the metric while failing the actual task, so precision/recall/F1 and their answer keys must be audited rather than accepted.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Aggregate metrics like F1 hide the asymmetry between over-fetch (context bloat, cost, downstream confusion) and under-fetch (missing evidence). An eval whose scoring rule rewards recall will select for an agent whose behavior is unacceptable in production, so the metric can be aligned to the wrong objective while appearing rigorous.

evidence_quotes.text: Repeated runs are not independent tasks; relative score does not establish system reliability.
You must report quality, reliability, performance, and total cost together.

core_insights.generalization: For stochastic systems, treat distributional properties (variance, tail behavior across repeated trials) as a separately reported dimension of the result, not as noise to be averaged away.
core_insights.insight: Reliability cannot be inferred from a relative score: repeated runs of the same task are not independent outcomes, so score variance must be measured and reported separately from mean quality, alongside performance and total operating cost.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes evaluation reporting as a four-axis vector (quality, reliability, performance, total cost) rather than a single number. A system that is slightly worse on average but far tighter in run-to-run variance may be the correct production choice, and the reverse is undetectable from a single aggregate.

evidence_quotes.text: Public benchmarks provide a landscape shortlist but suffer from spikey training nature.
Internal evaluations should mirror actual product workflows and domain-specific tasks.
Public leaderboards help map the landscape, but internal evaluations

core_insights.generalization: External standardized benchmarks are filters for candidate sets; only workload-matched evaluations support deployment decisions.
core_insights.insight: Public benchmarks and internal evaluations serve different functions and should not substitute for one another: public benchmarks provide a landscape shortlist but are spiky from training exposure, while internal evals must mirror actual product workflows and domain tasks.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a defensible division of labor: public leaderboards for candidate elimination, internal evals for selection and regression. Using a leaderboard to make the final choice over-indexes on tasks whose 'spiky' exposure to training data does not reflect your domain's failure modes.

evidence_quotes.text: Approval gates and audit queues must actively enforce stopping rather than just logging warnings.

core_insights.generalization: Any approval, budget, or policy checkpoint must be a blocking precondition in the execution graph, not an emitted event; otherwise the failure mode is silent bypass under load.
core_insights.insight: Safety gates and audit queues only work if they have enforcement authority; a gate that logs a warning instead of halting execution is not a gate.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This relocates the gate from the observability/annotation plane into the control plane of execution. Human-in-the-loop designs decay into post-hoc auditing unless the runtime structurally blocks until approval, which means approval state must be a dependency of tool invocation rather than a recorded event.

deep_dives.why: A recall-oriented metric can reward over-fetching that bloats context and confuses downstream reasoning, so the eval can be internally rigorous while aligned to the wrong objective. The engineering consequence is that scoring rules must be derived from business costs and re-scored under alternate weightings before they are trusted.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Repeated runs are not independent tasks; relative score does not establish system reliability.
deep_dives.why: A single relative score hides run-to-run instability, and repeated runs are not independent tasks. Reporting variance separately lets teams choose a slightly lower-mean configuration with tighter tails, and prevents aggregate scores from overstating confidence in production behavior.

key_claims.claim: Lower observed cost does not imply the intended tool was used successfully.
key_claims.evidence: A 28% drop in observed cost does not mean the agent successfully used the intended tool.

key_claims.claim: Changing the evaluation harness can invert which model performs better on the same benchmark.
key_claims.evidence: Model rankings change dramatically when you switch the evaluation harness.
key_claims.verification_question: How frequently do pairwise model rankings reverse across harnesses on Terminal-Bench-4, and is the reversal effect size larger than seed variance?

key_claims.claim: Agents treat empty tool results as evidence of absence rather than as a signal that retrieval failed.
key_claims.evidence: Agents often trust empty tool results rather than realizing evidence is missing.
key_claims.verification_question: What is the conditional probability of a definitive answer given an empty tool return, and does an explicit 'empty means unknown' instruction reduce it?

key_claims.claim: Repeated runs of the same task are not independent, so relative scores do not establish reliability.
key_claims.evidence: Repeated runs are not independent tasks; relative score does not establish system reliability.
key_claims.verification_question: What is the within-task vs. between-task variance decomposition for repeated agent runs, and how much does it inflate confidence intervals on relative scores?

key_claims.claim: Evaluation results should be reported jointly on quality, reliability, performance, and total cost.
key_claims.evidence: You must report quality, reliability, performance, and total cost together.

key_claims.claim: High recall obtained by over-fetching can satisfy the metric while failing the business need.
key_claims.evidence: Pulling in too many files (low precision) can result in high recall while failing business needs.
key_claims.verification_question: How does downstream answer accuracy degrade as the ratio of retrieved-to-relevant files increases, holding the relevant set constant?

key_claims.claim: Approval gates that only log warnings fail to prevent faulty execution.
key_claims.evidence: Approval gates and audit queues must actively enforce stopping rather than just logging warnings.
key_claims.verification_question: What fraction of flagged agent actions proceed to execution under warning-only gates versus blocking gates?

key_claims.claim: Public benchmark scores are spiky because of training exposure and therefore poor final-selection signals.
key_claims.evidence: Public benchmarks provide a landscape shortlist but suffer from spikey training nature.
key_claims.verification_question: Does performance on public benchmark tasks predict performance on held-out domain-matched internal tasks, and how large is the rank correlation gap?

open_questions.question: How should harness-model interaction effects be characterized without re-running the full harness × model matrix for every combination?
open_questions.research_direction: Identify harness features (tool-call retry policy, context assembly order, error surfacing) that mediate model capability, then build a small diagnostic suite that predicts harness sensitivity cheaply instead of running full benchmarks.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary shows rankings invert across harnesses (Opus 5 on OpenHands, Astra on PI on Terminal-Bench-4) but gives no mechanism for predicting which harness-model pairs will invert, so the only known method is exhaustive paired re-evaluation.

open_questions.question: Can a runtime detect that an agent is 'trusting empty results' before the task completes, rather than from post-hoc trace review?
open_questions.research_direction: Define a missing-evidence invariant over the trace (required tool uncalled, or called and returned empty, followed by a definitive answer) and test whether an online checker can halt or re-prompt the agent at that transition.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary documents the failure ('Agents often trust empty tool results rather than realizing evidence is missing') as an observed behavior requiring downstream analysis, but proposes no runtime detection mechanism.

open_questions.question: What makes an internal evaluation's workload coverage adequate, and how should heterogeneous task families be weighted?
open_questions.research_direction: Prototype coverage accounting by sampling production traces into task families and measuring per-family score variance to decide whether a single aggregate score or a per-family vector is the correct reporting unit.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary recommends clustering tasks into families (bug fixing vs. feature building) and mirroring product workflows, but offers no criterion for sufficient coverage or aggregate weighting.

open_questions.question: How are scoring rules and answer keys validated against the business cost of each error type?
open_questions.research_direction: Build a metric-alignment check that maps false-positive and false-negative outcomes to explicit business costs and re-scores existing eval sets under alternate weightings to detect metric-induced behavior selection.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary shows scoring rules can reward behavior that fails business needs (precision vs. recall, grepping 295 files for 6) but does not specify a procedure for deriving or auditing metric weights and ground truth.

project_ideas.based_on: Agents often trust empty tool results rather than realizing evidence is missing.
project_ideas.hypothesis: An online invariant that flags a definitive answer following an empty return from a required tool will detect trust-empty-result failures with higher precision than post-hoc score review, and a blocking re-prompt will reduce the rate of definitive answers after empty evidence.
project_ideas.measurement: Rate of definitive answers after empty required-tool returns, false-positive guard triggers, task accuracy, and total cost across warning-only versus blocking modes.
project_ideas.name: Missing Evidence Guard
project_ideas.poc: Instrument the tool layer to tag required-tool calls, return status, and final-answer events; replay existing eval tasks with empty-result injection; compare warning-only logging against a blocking re-prompt at the tool-return-to-answer transition.

project_ideas.based_on: Model rankings change dramatically when you switch the evaluation harness.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A small set of harness-feature probes predicts pairwise model-rank inversions across harnesses better than public benchmark rank, allowing teams to shortlist production configurations without running the full harness × model matrix.
project_ideas.measurement: Rank-inversion prediction accuracy, rank correlation with full matrix results, and evaluation cost versus exhaustive paired runs.
project_ideas.name: Harness Sensitivity Probe
project_ideas.poc: Build two harness variants that differ in retry policy, context assembly order, and error surfacing; run two models on a subset of tasks; compare predicted inversions against full paired evaluations.

project_ideas.based_on: Pulling in too many files (low precision) can result in high recall while failing business needs.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Re-scoring an existing retrieval evaluation under business-cost weights that penalize over-fetching will change the selected agent or configuration relative to F1, demonstrating metric-induced behavior selection.
project_ideas.measurement: Configuration ranking change, over-fetch ratio, and the delta between metric-selected and business-cost-selected winners.
project_ideas.name: Metric Cost Re-Scorer
project_ideas.poc: Take an eval set with retrieval traces, map false positives and false negatives to explicit business costs, and re-rank configurations under F1 versus cost-weighted scoring.

project_ideas.based_on: Approval gates and audit queues must actively enforce stopping rather than just logging warnings.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A blocking approval dependency in the tool-call path reduces execution of flagged actions to zero, while a warning-only gate allows a nonzero fraction of flagged actions to proceed.
project_ideas.measurement: Fraction of flagged actions that execute, added latency from human review, and throughput impact under suspension.
project_ideas.name: Blocking Approval Gate Reference
project_ideas.poc: Implement two gate modes in a tool dispatcher, warning-only and blocking, and replay a set of flagged agent actions through both.

source.title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Stephanie Jarmak
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Evaluating, testing, and building trust in AI coding and business agents
  • Purpose: To provide AI engineers and teams with a rigorous, scientific framework for evaluating coding and business agents, understanding failure modes in tool use, and designing evaluation experiments around real-world business needs. Stephanie Jarmak discusses how to evaluate, test, and build trust in AI agents when stakes are high. Drawing on her background as a researcher and AI engineer at Omni Analytics, she frames the evaluation of agents not as a simple matter of trusting metrics, but as a scientific process of questioning how and why agents use tools, how harnesses affect outcomes, and how to balance automation with human review loops.

Topic Map

Introduction and Speaker Background

  • Explanation: Introduction of Stephanie Jarmak, AI Engineer at Omni Analytics, and her background spanning sourcegraph, benchmarking coding agents (CodeScale Benchmark), and astronomy research.
  • Key claims:
    • Talk title is about how to trust your agents, but is mainly about how to not trust your agents.
    • Research scientist background instills a mindset of relentlessly questioning everything.
  • Examples:
    • Building CodeScale Benchmark at Sourcegraph to test agents across complex codebases.
  • Terminology:
    • Omni Analytics
    • CodeScale Benchmark
    • Semantic layer
  • Why it matters: Establishes speaker credibility and sets the skeptical, scientific tone required for evaluating non-deterministic AI agent systems.

Case Study: Lower Cost, Retrieval Failure, and Untrusting the Numbers

  • Explanation: An analysis of an evaluation run on a code search MCP tool where modifying the prompt lowered cost by 28% but the agent still suffered from retrieval failure and trusted empty results.
  • Key claims:
    • A 28% drop in observed cost does not mean the agent successfully used the intended tool.
    • Agents often trust empty tool results rather than realizing evidence is missing.
  • Examples:
    • Modifying initial prompt to encourage tool usage resulted in lower cost but the agent still skipped using the tool.
  • Terminology:
    • MCP tool
    • Observed cost
    • Primary evaluation score
    • Retrieval failure
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that proxy metrics like cost reduction can be misleading if the underlying agent behavior (tool utilization) is fundamentally broken.

The Impact of the Evaluation Harness

  • Explanation: Comparing different harnesses (OpenHands vs. PI) and models (Claude Opus 5 vs. GPT-6 Astra) on Terminal-Bench-4 to show how harness changes alter model rankings.
  • Key claims:
    • Model rankings change dramatically when you switch the evaluation harness.
    • You must evaluate the specific configuration you will actually run in production.
  • Examples:
    • Astra outperforming Opus 5 when using the PI harness versus OpenHands.
  • Terminology:
    • Terminal-Bench-4
    • Evaluation harness
    • OpenHands
    • PI
    • Claude Opus 5
    • GPT-6 Astra
  • Why it matters: Highlights that evaluation results are deeply sensitive to the harness setup, meaning benchmark scores from third parties may not reflect custom production environments.

Public Benchmarks vs. Internal Evaluation

  • Explanation: Differentiating between public benchmarks (standardized reference for landscape comparison) and internal evaluations (product and process improvement).
  • Key claims:
    • Public benchmarks provide a landscape shortlist but suffer from spikey training nature.
    • Internal evaluations should mirror actual product workflows and domain-specific tasks.
  • Examples:
    • Law firms evaluating coding agents versus software development teams.
  • Terminology:
    • Public benchmarks
    • Internal evaluation
    • Spiky nature
    • Workflow coverage
  • Why it matters: Prevents organizations from over-indexing on generic leaderboard metrics that do not capture domain-specific failure modes.

Designing Experiments Around Decisions

  • Explanation: How to design experiments considering workload coverage, variation between runs, and harness-model pairings.
  • Key claims:
    • Repeated runs are not independent tasks; relative score does not establish system reliability.
    • You must report quality, reliability, performance, and total cost together.
  • Examples:
    • Clustering coding tasks into families like bug fixing vs. feature building.
  • Terminology:
    • Workload coverage
    • Variation between runs
    • Independent outcomes
    • Total operating cost
  • Why it matters: Provides a rigorous framework for experimentation that accounts for non-determinism and cost tradeoffs.

Tracing Evidence to Conclusions

  • Explanation: Following the pipeline from available evidence to called tools, returned results, and agent interpretation.
  • Key claims:
    • You need to test search limits and known-relevant evidence separately to see if evidence is actually used.
    • Better evidence can still go unused if the agent or harness fails to leverage it.
  • Examples:
    • Search-limits test versus evidence test.
  • Terminology:
    • Search-limits test
    • Evidence test
    • Traceability
    • Pipeline
  • Why it matters: Enables engineers to debug where in the pipeline an agent fails—whether information was unavailable, uncalled, unreturned, or misinterpreted.

Auditing Scoring Rules, Answer Keys, and Gates

  • Explanation: Examining why scoring rules (e.g., precision vs. recall) matter and how quality gates must enforce actual execution rather than just flagging errors.
  • Key claims:
    • Pulling in too many files (low precision) can result in high recall while failing business needs.
    • Approval gates and audit queues must actively enforce stopping rather than just logging warnings.
  • Examples:
    • Grepping 295 files when only 6 were needed.
  • Terminology:
    • F1-score
    • Precision
    • Recall
    • Quality gates
    • Audit queues
  • Why it matters: Ensures that evaluation metrics align with real business objectives and that safety gates actually prevent faulty execution.

Key Points

Do not trust proxy metrics blindly

  • Explanation: Lower costs or higher benchmark scores can mask underlying failures where agents fail to invoke required tools.
  • Evidence: A 28% reduction in observed cost on code search tasks while the agent missed relevant evidence and trusted empty results.
  • Practical implication: Always verify that tool utilization and operational mechanics match expectations alongside cost and performance metrics.

Harness selection dictates model ranking

  • Explanation: Changing the evaluation harness can invert model performance superiority.
  • Evidence: Terminal-Bench-4 results showing Opus 5 winning on OpenHands while Astra won on the PI harness.
  • Practical implication: Test models inside your exact production harness rather than relying on public leaderboard rankings.

Separate public benchmarks from internal evaluations

  • Explanation: Public leaderboards help map the landscape, but internal evaluations are required for product and process improvement.
  • Evidence: Spiky nature of model training makes public benchmarks unreliable for specific legal or enterprise use cases.
  • Practical implication: Build internal evaluation datasets that reflect your organization's unique workload families and task distribution.

Trace every step from evidence to conclusion

  • Explanation: Failures can occur at availability, invocation, return, or interpretation stages of an agentic workflow.
  • Evidence: Search-limit tests and evidence tests revealing that agents ignore available information due to harness constraints.
  • Practical implication: Maintain comprehensive trace logs and run ablation tests on evidence sources and components separately.

Enforce quality gates actively

  • Explanation: Logging or flagging errors in audit queues is insufficient if the agent proceeds without human intervention.
  • Evidence: Software factory audit trials showing approval queues finding faults but failing to enforce stopping conditions.
  • Practical implication: Decouple detection from enforcement so that safety gates have hard execution-stopping power when thresholds are breached.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Agent Evaluation & Traceability Pipeline

  • How it works: Traces agent execution across four stages—Available, Called, Returned, and Interpreted—combined with search-limits and evidence tests.
  • Components:
    • Available data/tools
    • Called actions
    • Returned values
    • Interpreted conclusions
    • Search-limits test
    • Evidence test
  • When to use: When debugging why an agent missed information or failed to execute a task correctly.

Autonomy Decision & Gate Framework

  • How it works: Balances workflow coverage, variation runs, and pairing configurations to determine when an agent can act autonomously versus when to escalate to a human.
  • Components:
    • Workload coverage (Task families)
    • Variation between runs
    • Configuration pairing (Harness x Model)
    • Validated evaluator & execution controls
    • Stop and escalate protocols
  • When to use: When deciding how much autonomy to grant an agent in production software or enterprise workflows.

Examples & Case Studies

A coding agent ran a code search query, missed relevant evidence, and trusted the empty result returned by the search tool, while overall cost dropped by 28%.

  • Illustrates: Cost reduction and positive evaluation scores can mask underlying retrieval and tool-use failures.
  • Lesson: Measure tool utilization and trace evidence paths rather than relying solely on aggregate cost and primary scores.

Testing Opus 5 and Astra on Terminal-Bench-4 using two different harnesses (OpenHands and PI) resulted in completely reversed performance rankings.

  • Illustrates: Harness design heavily influences model performance and benchmark outcomes.
  • Lesson: Evaluate models using the exact configuration and harness you plan to deploy in production.

An LLM coding agent searching a codebase returned 295 files when only 6 were relevant (high recall, terrible precision).

  • Illustrates: Standard metrics like recall can be misleading if the evaluation scoring rule does not penalize excessive retrieval.
  • Lesson: Audit your scoring rules and answer keys to ensure they match actual business requirements.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Review your agent evaluation pipelines to check if agents actually use required tools during runs.
    • Audit your scoring rules and metrics (such as precision vs recall) to ensure they align with business goals.
    • Test models inside your own harness rather than trusting public leaderboard rankings.

summary.markdown:
## Overview
- **Speaker**: Stephanie Jarmak
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Evaluating, testing, and building trust in AI coding and business agents
- **Purpose**: To provide AI engineers and teams with a rigorous, scientific framework for evaluating coding and business agents, understanding failure modes in tool use, and designing evaluation experiments around real-world business needs.
Stephanie Jarmak discusses how to evaluate, test, and build trust in AI agents when stakes are high. Drawing on her background as a researcher and AI engineer at Omni Analytics, she frames the evaluation of agents not as a simple matter of trusting metrics, but as a scientific process of questioning how and why agents use tools, how harnesses affect outcomes, and how to balance automation with human review loops.
## Topic Map
### Introduction and Speaker Background
- **Explanation**: Introduction of Stephanie Jarmak, AI Engineer at Omni Analytics, and her background spanning sourcegraph, benchmarking coding agents (CodeScale Benchmark), and astronomy research.
- **Key claims**:
  - Talk title is about how to trust your agents, but is mainly about how to not trust your agents.
  - Research scientist background instills a mindset of relentlessly questioning everything.
- **Examples**:
  - Building CodeScale Benchmark at Sourcegraph to test agents across complex codebases.
- **Terminology**:
  - Omni Analytics
  - CodeScale Benchmark
  - Semantic layer
- **Why it matters**: Establishes speaker credibility and sets the skeptical, scientific tone required for evaluating non-deterministic AI agent systems.
### Case Study: Lower Cost, Retrieval Failure, and Untrusting the Numbers
- **Explanation**: An analysis of an evaluation run on a code search MCP tool where modifying the prompt lowered cost by 28% but the agent still suffered from retrieval failure and trusted empty results.
- **Key claims**:
  - A 28% drop in observed cost does not mean the agent successfully used the intended tool.
  - Agents often trust empty tool results rather than realizing evidence is missing.
- **Examples**:
  - Modifying initial prompt to encourage tool usage resulted in lower cost but the agent still skipped using the tool.
- **Terminology**:
  - MCP tool
  - Observed cost
  - Primary evaluation score
  - Retrieval failure
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that proxy metrics like cost reduction can be misleading if the underlying agent behavior (tool utilization) is fundamentally broken.
### The Impact of the Evaluation Harness
- **Explanation**: Comparing different harnesses (OpenHands vs. PI) and models (Claude Opus 5 vs. GPT-6 Astra) on Terminal-Bench-4 to show how harness changes alter model rankings.
- **Key claims**:
  - Model rankings change dramatically when you switch the evaluation harness.
  - You must evaluate the specific configuration you will actually run in production.
- **Examples**:
  - Astra outperforming Opus 5 when using the PI harness versus OpenHands.
- **Terminology**:
  - Terminal-Bench-4
  - Evaluation harness
  - OpenHands
  - PI
  - Claude Opus 5
  - GPT-6 Astra
- **Why it matters**: Highlights that evaluation results are deeply sensitive to the harness setup, meaning benchmark scores from third parties may not reflect custom production environments.
### Public Benchmarks vs. Internal Evaluation
- **Explanation**: Differentiating between public benchmarks (standardized reference for landscape comparison) and internal evaluations (product and process improvement).
- **Key claims**:
  - Public benchmarks provide a landscape shortlist but suffer from spikey training nature.
  - Internal evaluations should mirror actual product workflows and domain-specific tasks.
- **Examples**:
  - Law firms evaluating coding agents versus software development teams.
- **Terminology**:
  - Public benchmarks
  - Internal evaluation
  - Spiky nature
  - Workflow coverage
- **Why it matters**: Prevents organizations from over-indexing on generic leaderboard metrics that do not capture domain-specific failure modes.
### Designing Experiments Around Decisions
- **Explanation**: How to design experiments considering workload coverage, variation between runs, and harness-model pairings.
- **Key claims**:
  - Repeated runs are not independent tasks; relative score does not establish system reliability.
  - You must report quality, reliability, performance, and total cost together.
- **Examples**:
  - Clustering coding tasks into families like bug fixing vs. feature building.
- **Terminology**:
  - Workload coverage
  - Variation between runs
  - Independent outcomes
  - Total operating cost
- **Why it matters**: Provides a rigorous framework for experimentation that accounts for non-determinism and cost tradeoffs.
### Tracing Evidence to Conclusions
- **Explanation**: Following the pipeline from available evidence to called tools, returned results, and agent interpretation.
- **Key claims**:
  - You need to test search limits and known-relevant evidence separately to see if evidence is actually used.
  - Better evidence can still go unused if the agent or harness fails to leverage it.
- **Examples**:
  - Search-limits test versus evidence test.
- **Terminology**:
  - Search-limits test
  - Evidence test
  - Traceability
  - Pipeline
- **Why it matters**: Enables engineers to debug where in the pipeline an agent fails—whether information was unavailable, uncalled, unreturned, or misinterpreted.
### Auditing Scoring Rules, Answer Keys, and Gates
- **Explanation**: Examining why scoring rules (e.g., precision vs. recall) matter and how quality gates must enforce actual execution rather than just flagging errors.
- **Key claims**:
  - Pulling in too many files (low precision) can result in high recall while failing business needs.
  - Approval gates and audit queues must actively enforce stopping rather than just logging warnings.
- **Examples**:
  - Grepping 295 files when only 6 were needed.
- **Terminology**:
  - F1-score
  - Precision
  - Recall
  - Quality gates
  - Audit queues
- **Why it matters**: Ensures that evaluation metrics align with real business objectives and that safety gates actually prevent faulty execution.
## Key Points
### Do not trust proxy metrics blindly
- **Explanation**: Lower costs or higher benchmark scores can mask underlying failures where agents fail to invoke required tools.
- **Evidence**: A 28% reduction in observed cost on code search tasks while the agent missed relevant evidence and trusted empty results.
- **Practical implication**: Always verify that tool utilization and operational mechanics match expectations alongside cost and performance metrics.
### Harness selection dictates model ranking
- **Explanation**: Changing the evaluation harness can invert model performance superiority.
- **Evidence**: Terminal-Bench-4 results showing Opus 5 winning on OpenHands while Astra won on the PI harness.
- **Practical implication**: Test models inside your exact production harness rather than relying on public leaderboard rankings.
### Separate public benchmarks from internal evaluations
- **Explanation**: Public leaderboards help map the landscape, but internal evaluations are required for product and process improvement.
- **Evidence**: Spiky nature of model training makes public benchmarks unreliable for specific legal or enterprise use cases.
- **Practical implication**: Build internal evaluation datasets that reflect your organization's unique workload families and task distribution.
### Trace every step from evidence to conclusion
- **Explanation**: Failures can occur at availability, invocation, return, or interpretation stages of an agentic workflow.
- **Evidence**: Search-limit tests and evidence tests revealing that agents ignore available information due to harness constraints.
- **Practical implication**: Maintain comprehensive trace logs and run ablation tests on evidence sources and components separately.
### Enforce quality gates actively
- **Explanation**: Logging or flagging errors in audit queues is insufficient if the agent proceeds without human intervention.
- **Evidence**: Software factory audit trials showing approval queues finding faults but failing to enforce stopping conditions.
- **Practical implication**: Decouple detection from enforcement so that safety gates have hard execution-stopping power when thresholds are breached.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Agent Evaluation & Traceability Pipeline
- **How it works**: Traces agent execution across four stages—Available, Called, Returned, and Interpreted—combined with search-limits and evidence tests.
- **Components**:
  - Available data/tools
  - Called actions
  - Returned values
  - Interpreted conclusions
  - Search-limits test
  - Evidence test
- **When to use**: When debugging why an agent missed information or failed to execute a task correctly.
### Autonomy Decision & Gate Framework
- **How it works**: Balances workflow coverage, variation runs, and pairing configurations to determine when an agent can act autonomously versus when to escalate to a human.
- **Components**:
  - Workload coverage (Task families)
  - Variation between runs
  - Configuration pairing (Harness x Model)
  - Validated evaluator & execution controls
  - Stop and escalate protocols
- **When to use**: When deciding how much autonomy to grant an agent in production software or enterprise workflows.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A coding agent ran a code search query, missed relevant evidence, and trusted the empty result returned by the search tool, while overall cost dropped by 28%.
- **Illustrates**: Cost reduction and positive evaluation scores can mask underlying retrieval and tool-use failures.
- **Lesson**: Measure tool utilization and trace evidence paths rather than relying solely on aggregate cost and primary scores.
### Testing Opus 5 and Astra on Terminal-Bench-4 using two different harnesses (OpenHands and PI) resulted in completely reversed performance rankings.
- **Illustrates**: Harness design heavily influences model performance and benchmark outcomes.
- **Lesson**: Evaluate models using the exact configuration and harness you plan to deploy in production.
### An LLM coding agent searching a codebase returned 295 files when only 6 were relevant (high recall, terrible precision).
- **Illustrates**: Standard metrics like recall can be misleading if the evaluation scoring rule does not penalize excessive retrieval.
- **Lesson**: Audit your scoring rules and answer keys to ensure they match actual business requirements.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Review your agent evaluation pipelines to check if agents actually use required tools during runs.
  - Audit your scoring rules and metrics (such as precision vs recall) to ensure they align with business goals.
  - Test models inside your own harness rather than trusting public leaderboard rankings.
- **Strategic**:
  - Establish internal evaluation benchmarks tailored to your organization's specific task families and workloads.
  - Design experiments to capture total operating cost, reliability, and workload coverage together.
  - Enforce hard execution gates rather than relying solely on audit logs and human review queues.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - Are our evaluation harness configurations identical to our production deployment environment?
  - How do our agents behave when search tools return empty results?
  - Do our quality gates actively stop execution when faults are detected, or do they just log warnings?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Model rankings on coding benchmarks like Terminal-Bench-4 invert when switching between OpenHands and PI harnesses. (empirical)
- Agents frequently trust empty search results rather than recognizing missing retrieval evidence. (behavioral)
- A 1% false alarm rate in automated AI audit tools can generate 10,000 manual reviews on 1 million actions, exceeding domain expert capacity. (statistical)
## Notable Quotes
> "It says how to trust your agents, but I think largely this talk is mainly about how to not trust your agents." (at 0:12)
> "Production is truth." (at 23:59)
## Compressed Summary
- Do not trust aggregate cost or benchmark scores blindly; verify tool utilization and evidence paths.
- Evaluation harnesses significantly alter model performance rankings; test in your exact production setup.
- Separate public benchmarks for landscape mapping from internal evaluations for product improvement.
- Trace execution steps from availability to interpretation to identify exact points of failure.
- Enforce hard execution stops in quality gates rather than relying solely on passive audit logs.
- **Keywords**: agent evaluation, benchmarking, harness traceability, reliability, tool use
- **Core insight**: Evaluating AI agents requires a scientific, skeptical mindset that goes beyond proxy metrics and public benchmarks to audit actual harness behavior, evidence traceability, and active enforcement controls.
